Source slide page 1 (extracted text):
Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB
Introduction to MATLAB, Commands, Variables & Plotting

Introduction • Commands • Variables • 2D & 3D Plotting

1

Source slide page 2 (extracted text):
2. Learning Objectives

• Identify the main parts of the MATLAB user interface.
• Use basic commands and assign values to variables.
• Create and customize 2D Cartesian and polar plots.
• Create introductory 3D curves and surfaces.
• Add titles, axis labels, legends, grids and curve labels.
• Modify and edit plots to communicate results clearly.

Goal: learn by typing, running, observing and changing MATLAB code.

2

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 3 (extracted text):
3. What is MATLAB?

• MATLAB = MATrix LABoratory.
• A programming and numerical-computing environment used by engineers and scientists.
• Works naturally with vectors, matrices, equations, data and graphs.
• Provides built-in functions for mathematics, visualization, simulation and modelling.

Think of MATLAB as a calculator + programming environment + visualization tool.

3

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 4 (extracted text):
4. Why MATLAB for Engineering Students?

• Solve mathematical problems quickly.
• Visualize functions and data instead of only calculating numbers.
• Experiment by changing parameters and immediately seeing the effect.
• Build a foundation for ODEs, PDEs, signal processing, AI/ML and engineering simulation.

MATLAB is especially useful when mathematics and computation need to work together.

4

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 5 (extracted text):
5. MATLAB User Interface

Main areas

Also useful

• Command Window – type and execute commands.
• Workspace – view variables currently in memory.
• Current Folder – manage files and folders.
• Command History – revisit previously executed commands.

• Editor – write and save scripts.
• Figure Window – display plots.
• Toolstrip – access common commands and tools.
• Layout can be customized for your workflow.

5

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 6 (extracted text):
6. Command Window

The Command Window is the quickest place to test MATLAB commands.  The prompt >> means MATLAB is ready for input.
 Try it:
Calculate 12^2, log(10), cos(pi).

>> 2 + 3
ans =
     5

>> sqrt(25)
ans =
     5

>> sin(pi/2)
ans =
     1

6

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 7 (extracted text):
7. Workspace

What you see

Example

• Variable name
• Value
• Size
• Class / data type

• Enter: x = 25
• MATLAB creates x.
• The Workspace shows x and its value.
• Variables remain available until cleared.

7

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 8 (extracted text):
8. Current Folder

The Current Folder tells MATLAB where files are being stored or searched for.  Use pwd to display the current folder and ls to list its contents.
 Try it:
Use pwd. Identify your current working folder.

pwd

ls

cd('C:\MATLAB\MyFiles')

8

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 9 (extracted text):
9. Command History & Editor

Command History stores commands you have already executed.  The Editor is useful when several commands must be run together as a script.  A semicolon suppresses output.
 Try it:
Create a script containing three calculations.

a = 10;
b = 20;
c = a + b;

% Save these commands as a script
% Example: first_program.m

9

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 10 (extracted text):
10. Your First MATLAB Program

A simple script can combine commands, variables and formatted output.  clc clears the Command Window; clear removes variables from the Workspace.
 Try it:
Change the name and marks and run the script.

clc
clear

name = 'MATLAB';
marks = 85;

fprintf('Welcome to %s!\n', name)
fprintf('Marks = %d\n', marks)

10

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 11 (extracted text):
11. Basic Arithmetic Commands

MATLAB follows standard mathematical notation.  Use * for multiplication, / for division and ^ for powers.
 Try it:
Evaluate 15/4, 3^4 and sqrt(144).

a = 12;
b = 5;

a + b
a - b
a * b
a / b
a^2
sqrt(a)
log(a)
exp(a)

11

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 13 (extracted text):
13. Common Mathematical Functions

MATLAB has many built-in mathematical functions.  For trigonometric functions, MATLAB uses radians.
 Try it:
Find sin(30°) correctly using pi/6.

sin(pi/2)
cos(0)
tan(pi/4)

sqrt(49)
abs(-12)
log(10)
log10(1000)
exp(1)

13

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 14 (extracted text):
14. Vectors – Row and Column

Vectors store a sequence of values.  [ ] creates vectors. The colon operator is a convenient way to generate equally spaced values.
 Try it:
Create values from 0 to 20 with a step of 2.

x = [1 2 3 4 5]

y = [1; 2; 3; 4; 5]

x = 0:1:10

t = 0:0.1:1

14

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 15 (extracted text):
15. Matrices – Basic Introduction

MATLAB is built around matrices and arrays.  Rows are separated by semicolons; columns by spaces.
 Try it:
Create a 3×3 matrix and display its second row.

A = [1 2 3; 4 5 6]

size(A)
A(1,2)
A(:,2)
A(2,:)

15

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 16 (extracted text):
16. Useful MATLAB Commands

These commands help you organize and debug your MATLAB session.
 Try it:
Run who and whos after creating three variables.

clc       % clear Command Window
clear     % clear variables
who       % list variables
whos      % detailed variable list
close all % close figures
help plot  % get help

% Comments begin with %

16

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 17 (extracted text):
17. What is Plotting?

Plotting converts numerical values into a visual graph.  A basic plot needs x-values and corresponding y-values.  The plot command creates a 2D Cartesian graph.
 Try it:
Replace sin(x) with cos(x).

x = 0:0.1:2*pi;
y = sin(x);
plot(x,y)

17

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 18 (extracted text):
18. Basic 2D Cartesian Plot

The horizontal axis is x and the vertical axis is y.  The smaller the step size, the smoother the displayed curve usually becomes.
 Try it:
Plot y = x^2 for -5 ≤ x ≤ 5.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);

plot(x,y)
grid on

18

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 19 (extracted text):
19. Title and Axis Labels

Good graphs tell the reader what is being plotted.  Always label axes and give the graph a meaningful title.
 Try it:
Label a graph of y = x^2 with units if appropriate.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);

plot(x,y)
xlabel('x')
ylabel('sin(x)')
title('Sine Curve')
grid on

19

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 20 (extracted text):
20. Grid, Legend & Line Properties

Common plot properties include line color, line width and line style.  A legend identifies curves when more than one curve is present.
 Try it:
Try '--' for a dashed line.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
plot(x,sin(x),'b','LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Sine Curve')
legend('sin(x)')

20

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 21 (extracted text):
21. Multiple Curves in One Plot

hold on lets you add another curve to the same axes.  hold off returns MATLAB to the normal plotting behavior.
 Try it:
Add y = sin(2x) to the same graph.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y1 = sin(x);
y2 = cos(x);

plot(x,y1,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold on
plot(x,y2,'LineWidth',1.5)
hold off

grid on
legend('sin(x)','cos(x)')
xlabel('x')
ylabel('Value')
title('Sine and Cosine')

21

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 22 (extracted text):
22. Curve Labelling & Editing

MATLAB Figure tools allow interactive editing.  You can inspect and modify plot properties, labels, axes and curves without rewriting everything.
 Try it:
Open the Figure window and identify the plot editing tools.

x = 0:0.01:2*pi;
y = sin(x);
plot(x,y,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
title('Interactive Curve Editing')

% You can also use the Figure
% window tools to edit labels,
% lines and axes.

22

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 23 (extracted text):
23. 2D Polar Plot

Polar coordinates use radius r and angle θ instead of x and y.  polarplot(theta,r) is designed for polar graphs.
 Try it:
Try r = 2*cos(theta). What shape do you get?

theta = 0:0.01:2*pi;
r = 1 + cos(theta);

polarplot(theta,r)
title('Cardioid')

23

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 24 (extracted text):
24. Cartesian vs Polar Plot

Cartesian

Polar

• Coordinates: (x, y)
• Horizontal and vertical axes
• Use plot(x,y)
• Useful for y = f(x)

• Coordinates: (r, θ)
• Radius and angle
• Use polarplot(θ,r)
• Useful for circular/radial patterns

24

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 25 (extracted text):
25. Introduction to 3D Plotting

A 3D curve uses x, y and z coordinates.  plot3 creates a three-dimensional line plot.
 Try it:
Rotate the Figure using the interactive 3D controls.

t = 0:0.01:10*pi;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t;

plot3(x,y,z)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Helix')

25

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 26 (extracted text):
26. 3D Cartesian Curve

Parametric curves define x, y and z using a common parameter t.  Changing the equations changes the shape of the curve.
 Try it:
Change z = t/3 to z = t/6 and observe the effect.

t = 0:0.02:20;
x = cos(t);
y = sin(t);
z = t/3;

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',1.5)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('3D Parametric Curve')

26

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 27 (extracted text):
27. 3D Surface Plot

A surface is defined over a grid of X and Y values.  meshgrid creates the coordinate grid and surf displays the surface.
 Try it:
Try Z = sin(sqrt(X.^2 + Y.^2)).

[X,Y] = meshgrid(-5:0.2:5);
Z = X.^2 + Y.^2;

surf(X,Y,Z)
shading interp
grid on
xlabel('X')
ylabel('Y')
zlabel('Z')
title('Paraboloid Surface')

27

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 28 (extracted text):
28. 3D Polar / Cylindrical Visualization

MATLAB can convert polar/cylindrical coordinates into Cartesian coordinates for 3D visualization.  x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
 Try it:
Change 0.2 to 0.5 and observe the shape.

theta = 0:0.05:2*pi;
r = 1 + 0.2*cos(3*theta);

x = r.*cos(theta);
y = r.*sin(theta);
z = zeros(size(theta));

plot3(x,y,z,'LineWidth',2)
grid on
xlabel('x')
ylabel('y')
zlabel('z')
title('Polar Curve in 3D Axes')

28

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 29 (extracted text):
29. Mini Hands-on Exercise

Task A – 2D

Task B – 3D

• Plot y = x² for -5 ≤ x ≤ 5.
• Add title, x-label, y-label and grid.
• Change the line width.
• Add a legend.

• Create a 3D helix.
• Label x, y and z axes.
• Add a title and grid.
• Rotate the graph and observe it from different views.

29

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech

Source slide page 30 (extracted text):
30. Summary & Practice Tasks

• MATLAB provides an interactive environment for engineering computation.
• Variables, vectors and matrices form the foundation of MATLAB.
• plot and polarplot create 2D graphs; plot3 and surf create 3D visualizations.
• Use xlabel, ylabel, zlabel, title, legend and grid on to improve graphs.
• Practice by changing parameters and predicting how the graph will change.

Practice: plot y = sin(x), y = cos(x), a polar cardioid, a 3D helix and a 3D surface.

30

Hands-on Learning Using MATLAB  •  First-Year B.Tech
